questions.q: Which gestational weeks constitute the fetal period of human development, characterized primarily by rapid growth and functional maturation of existing organs?
options: From week 9 after fertilisation until birth
questions.explain: The fetal period begins at the start of the 9th week after fertilization and continues until birth (typically 38 weeks post-fertilization or 40 weeks from the last menstrual period), marked by rapid somatic growth and tissue maturation.

open.q: At which post-fertilization week does the fetal period begin?

questions.q: During which fetal week do the external genitalia differentiate sufficiently to allow reliable morphological sex determination on gross inspection and ultrasonography?
questions.explain: Although chromosomal sex is determined at fertilization, external genitalia look identical until week 9 and become clearly distinguishable as male or female by the end of week 12.

open.q: By which week of development are the external genitalia sufficiently differentiated to be reliably distinguished as male or female?

questions.q: During which week do the physiologically herniated midgut loops normally return from the umbilical cord into the abdominal cavity and complete their 270-degree counterclockwise rotation?
questions.explain: The midgut herniates into the proximal umbilical cord during week 6 and retracts back into the enlarging abdominal cavity during week 10; failure of return causes an omphalocele.

open.q: In which developmental week do the intestinal loops return into the abdominal cavity from physiological umbilical herniation?

questions.q: Which sebaceous gland secretion and desquamated epithelial cell coating protects the fetal skin from maceration and chapping by amniotic fluid during the second half of pregnancy?
questions.explain: Vernix caseosa is a white, greasy biofilm composed of sebum and shed periderm cells that covers the fetal skin starting around weeks 17–20 to protect it against continuous exposure to amniotic fluid.

open.q: Name the white, cheesy protective lipid-rich coating covering the fetal skin during the second half of gestation.

questions.q: What is the fine, downy hair covering the fetal body around week 20 that helps anchor the vernix caseosa to the skin and is mostly shed before birth?
questions.explain: Lanugo is fine, unpigmented fetal hair appearing around week 20 that holds vernix caseosa onto the skin; it is normally shed before full-term birth (except in premature infants).

open.q: Name the fine, downy fetal hair that appears around week 20 and helps retain vernix caseosa on the skin.

questions.q: What is the clinical term for the first fetal movements perceived by the mother, typically occurring between weeks 17 and 20 of pregnancy?
questions.explain: Quickening refers to the first maternal perception of active fetal limb movements, usually felt around week 17 in multiparous women and weeks 18–20 in primigravidae.

open.q: What clinical term describes the mother's first perception of fetal movements around weeks 17–20?

questions.q: At approximately which post-fertilization week do type II pneumocytes begin secreting sufficient pulmonary surfactant to allow potential extrauterine survival (fetal viability threshold) with neonatal intensive care?
options: Approximately weeks 22–24, during the canalicular stage
questions.explain: Around weeks 22–24, terminal bronchioles branch into respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts (canalicular stage) and type II pneumocytes begin producing surfactant, marking the lower limit of extrauterine fetal viability.

open.q: Around which post-fertilization weeks do type II alveolar cells begin secreting pulmonary surfactant, establishing the threshold of fetal viability?

questions.q: During the final two months of gestation (weeks 30 to 38), which metabolic tissue accumulates rapidly in the subcutaneous layer to provide energy reserves and thermal insulation after birth?
questions.explain: While brown fat forms earlier (weeks 17–20) for non-shivering thermogenesis, white subcutaneous fat is deposited rapidly during the last 6–8 weeks of gestation, smoothing out wrinkled fetal skin and accounting for ~16% of term body weight.

open.q: Which type of adipose tissue is deposited rapidly in the subcutaneous layer during the last 6–8 weeks of gestation to round out fetal contours?

questions.q: What are the maternal and fetal components that form the definitive human placenta?
options: Decidua basalis from the mother and chorion frondosum from the fetus
questions.explain: At the embryonic pole, chorionic villi proliferate into the brush-like chorion frondosum (villous chorion), which interdigitates with the underlying endometrial decidua basalis to form the placenta.

open.q: Name the maternal endometrial component and the fetal chorionic component that together constitute the placenta.

questions.q: Which four tissue layers separate maternal blood in the intervillous space from fetal blood inside the villous capillaries in the early placental barrier (before week 20)?
options: Syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, villous connective tissue and fetal capillary endothelium
Endometrial epithelium, decidua parietalis, amnion and yolk sac
Syncytiotrophoblast, zona pellucida, myometrium and maternal endothelium
Cytotrophoblast, Wharton's jelly, allantois and chorion laeve
questions.explain: In early pregnancy, the placental membrane consists of syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast (Langhans layer), extraembryonic mesoderm core, and fetal capillary endothelium; after week 20, cytotrophoblast degenerates in most villi, thinning the barrier to enhance exchange.

open.q: List the four histological layers of the placental barrier separating maternal and fetal blood prior to week 20.
accept: syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, villous connective tissue, and fetal capillary endothelium
syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, extraembryonic mesoderm, fetal endothelium

questions.q: What are the 15 to 20 lobulated compartments on the maternal surface of a delivered full-term placenta separated by decidual septa called?
questions.explain: Decidual septa project upward from the basal plate toward (but not reaching) the chorionic plate, dividing the maternal surface of the placenta into 15–20 slightly bulging lobes called cotyledons, each containing two or more stem villi.

open.q: Name the 15–20 lobular subdivisions visible on the maternal surface of a term placenta separated by decidual septa.

questions.q: Which class of maternal immunoglobulin crosses the placental barrier via FcRn receptor-mediated transcytosis in the syncytiotrophoblast to confer passive immunity to the newborn?
questions.explain: Maternal IgG antibodies are selectively transported across the syncytiotrophoblast via neonatal Fc receptors (FcRn) during the third trimester, providing passive humoral immunity for the first 3–6 months of postnatal life; IgM does not cross the placenta.

open.q: Which specific class of maternal antibodies crosses the placenta to provide passive immunity to the fetus?

questions.q: Why must the fetal adrenal cortex and placenta cooperate ('fetoplacental unit') to synthesize estriol during pregnancy?
options: The placenta lacks CYP17; fetal adrenal DHEA-S supplies the estriol precursor
The placenta cannot synthesise progesterone from cholesterol
Maternal ovaries produce all estriol throughout late pregnancy
questions.explain: The placenta lacks 17-alpha-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase; therefore, the fetal adrenal cortex produces dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-S), which is 16-alpha-hydroxylated in the fetal liver and aromatized by the placenta into estriol.

open.q: Which androgen precursor produced by the fetal adrenal cortex is converted by the fetal liver and placenta into estriol?

questions.q: Following a difficult vaginal delivery, inspection of the maternal surface of the placenta reveals a missing cotyledon, and the patient develops brisk postpartum hemorrhage. Why does a retained cotyledon cause severe uterine bleeding?
options: Retained tissue prevents myometrial contraction and placental-bed vessel compression
The cotyledon secretes heparin into the maternal circulation
The cotyledon causes immediate rupture of the uterine artery
questions.explain: Hemostasis after placental separation depends on sustained contraction of the interlacing 'living ligature' myometrial fibers compressing the endometrial spiral arteries; retained placental fragments prevent uterine contraction and cause postpartum hemorrhage.

open.q: What is the primary physiological mechanism by which postpartum bleeding from maternal spiral arteries is halted immediately after placental delivery?

questions.q: A 34-year-old woman with two prior cesarean deliveries undergoes an elective repeat cesarean section, during which the placenta fails to separate cleanly because chorionic villi attach directly to the myometrium without an intervening decidua basalis. What is this condition called?
questions.explain: Defective decidualization (often over a prior uterine scar) allows chorionic villi to adhere directly to the myometrium (placenta accreta), invade into the myometrium (placenta increta), or penetrate through the uterine serosa (placenta percreta).

open.q: What term describes abnormal adherence of chorionic villi directly to the myometrium due to absence of the decidua basalis?

questions.q: What is the normal vascular composition of a mature human umbilical cord?
options: Two umbilical arteries and one left umbilical vein surrounded by Wharton jelly
Two umbilical veins and one umbilical artery
One umbilical artery and one right umbilical vein
Three umbilical arteries and two umbilical veins
questions.explain: The mature umbilical cord contains two umbilical arteries (carrying deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta) and one left umbilical vein (carrying oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus), cushioned by mucoid Wharton jelly.

open.q: State the normal number and type of blood vessels present in a mature human umbilical cord.
accept: two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein

questions.q: Discovery of a single umbilical artery (two-vessel cord) on routine prenatal ultrasound warrants a targeted fetal anatomical survey because it is associated with a 15–20% risk of:
questions.explain: Absence of one umbilical artery occurs in ~1% of singleton births and is associated with underlying structural anomalies, most notably congenital heart defects and renal/urinary tract malformations.

open.q: Which two major organ systems most commonly exhibit associated congenital anomalies when a fetus has a single umbilical artery?

questions.q: During the second half of pregnancy, what are the primary physiological source and primary route of clearance of amniotic fluid?
options: Produced primarily by fetal urine excretion and cleared primarily by fetal swallowing
Produced by maternal sweat glands and cleared by umbilical arteries
Produced by the yolk sac and cleared by the allantois
Produced by fetal bile and cleared by maternal lymphatics
questions.explain: In early gestation, amniotic fluid derives from maternal plasma transudate and amniotic epithelium; from mid-gestation onward, fetal kidneys excrete ~500 mL/day of hypotonic urine into the amniotic sac while the fetus swallows ~500 mL/day, which is absorbed by the gut and transferred to maternal blood across the placenta.

open.q: During the second half of gestation, how is amniotic fluid primarily produced and how is it primarily removed?
accept: produced by fetal urine and cleared by fetal swallowing

questions.q: An obstetric ultrasound at 28 weeks gestation shows severe oligohydramnios (amniotic fluid index < 5 cm). Fetal bilateral renal agenesis is diagnosed, resulting in pulmonary hypoplasia, limb deformities, and flattened facial features (Potter sequence). Why does oligohydramnios cause pulmonary hypoplasia?
options: Oligohydramnios compresses the thorax and limits normal lung growth
Excess fluid floods the fetal trachea
The diaphragm cannot form without fetal urine
questions.explain: Normal fetal lung growth requires adequate intraluminal fluid pressure and unrestricted thoracic expansion in an adequate amniotic fluid space; severe oligohydramnios compresses the chest and reduces lung liquid retention, causing fatal pulmonary hypoplasia.

open.q: What life-threatening respiratory complication develops in a fetus exposed to prolonged severe oligohydramnios (as in Potter sequence)?

questions.q: A 29-year-old pregnant woman at 32 weeks gestation presents with rapid uterine enlargement and severe polyhydramnios (amniotic fluid > 2,000 mL). Which fetal congenital anomaly is a classic cause of polyhydramnios due to impaired fetal swallowing or gastrointestinal absorption?
options: Esophageal atresia or duodenal atresia (or anencephaly)
questions.explain: Polyhydramnios occurs when the fetus cannot swallow or absorb amniotic fluid—classically caused by upper GI obstruction (esophageal or duodenal atresia) or CNS defects impairing the swallowing reflex (anencephaly)—or in maternal diabetes mellitus.

open.q: Name two fetal congenital anomalies that cause polyhydramnios by preventing normal swallowing or intestinal absorption of amniotic fluid.

questions.q: Which three vascular shunts in the fetal circulation bypass the non-functioning fetal lungs and partially bypass the fetal liver?
options: Ductus venosus, foramen ovale, and ductus arteriosus
Ligamentum teres, ligamentum venosum, and medial umbilical ligaments
Aortic arch, pulmonary trunk, and coronary sinus
Superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, and portal vein
questions.explain: In the fetus, the ductus venosus shunts oxygenated umbilical venous blood past the liver sinusoids to the IVC; the foramen ovale shunts right atrial blood into the left atrium; and the ductus arteriosus shunts pulmonary trunk blood into the descending aorta.

open.q: Name the three anatomical shunts characteristic of the fetal circulation.
accept: ductus venosus, foramen ovale, and ductus arteriosus
foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus, and ductus venosus

questions.q: Where in the fetal circulatory system is the oxygen saturation of blood highest?
questions.explain: The single umbilical vein carries freshly oxygenated blood (~80% oxygen saturation) directly from the placental villi toward the fetal liver and ductus venosus, whereas umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood (~58% saturation) back to the placenta.

open.q: Which blood vessel in the fetal circulation carries blood with the highest oxygen saturation?

questions.q: What are the adult fibrous remnants of the fetal umbilical vein, ductus venosus, and ductus arteriosus respectively?
options: Ligamentum teres hepatis (round ligament of liver), ligamentum venosum, and ligamentum arteriosum
Medial umbilical ligaments, median umbilical ligament, and fossa ovalis
Falciform ligament, coronary ligament, and ligamentum flavum
Ligamentum nuchae, inguinal ligament, and pectineal ligament
questions.explain: After birth, the umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres hepatis, the ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum, the ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum, the foramen ovale closes to form the fossa ovalis, and the distal umbilical arteries become the medial umbilical ligaments.

open.q: What adult anatomical structure does the fetal ductus venosus become after postnatal obliteration?

questions.q: Which two physiological events at birth trigger functional closure of the ductus arteriosus within the first 24 to 48 hours of postnatal life?
options: Higher PaO2 and lower PGE2 trigger ductus arteriosus constriction
Increase in maternal estrogen and drop in fetal cortisol
Closure of the umbilical arteries and drop in systemic vascular resistance
Surge in fetal erythropoietin and drop in PaO2
questions.explain: Expansion of the lungs at the first breath sharply raises arterial PaO2 (stimulating smooth muscle contraction in the ductus wall), while removal of the placenta eliminates the major source of vasodilatory PGE2, causing functional closure of the ductus arteriosus.

open.q: Which two key physiological changes at birth stimulate smooth muscle constriction and functional closure of the ductus arteriosus?
accept: increased oxygen tension and decreased prostaglandin E2
rise in PaO2 and drop in PGE2

questions.q: Which posterior pituitary nonapeptide hormone stimulates rhythmic myometrial contractions during parturition and triggers contraction of mammary myoepithelial cells for milk ejection?
questions.explain: Oxytocin is synthesized in the hypothalamic paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei, released from the neurohypophysis in response to cervical stretch (Ferguson reflex) and infant suckling, and stimulates uterine smooth muscle and mammary myoepithelial cells.

open.q: Name the neurohypophyseal hormone that drives uterine myometrial contractions during labor and milk let-down during breastfeeding.
